text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game — I'm weighing the payoffs of keeping tokens privately versus contributing to the group. Keeping a token gives me 1 point but costs the other three members 0.3 each, while contributing gives everyone, including me, 0.3 points. I'm working out that my total score depends on my own choice plus the sum of what others keep privately, since each private token others hold reduces my points by 0.3.

Since a private token always yields more to me individually (1 vs 0.3) regardless of what others do, keeping everything private is the dominant strategy, even though full cooperation (everyone contributing everything) would yield higher payoffs for everyone (6 each vs 2 each under full defection). I'm now considering whether repeated rounds and reciprocity could shift behavior away from the one-shot Nash equilibrium of total defection.

Given the risk that full group contribution leaves me vulnerable to free-riders, I think a moderate opening move — contributing around 10 out of 20 to the group fund — makes sense as a way to signal willingness to cooperate while limiting exposure if others defect.

So keeping tokens is individually dominant (1 > 0.3 per token regardless of others' choices), yet if everyone keeps everything, each ends up with only a net 2 points after externalities, compared to 6 points each if everyone contributed fully. This is a classic dominant-strategy-versus-social-optimum tension, though it depends on whether this is repeated or one-shot.

Given it's repeated over 10 rounds without a direct punishment mechanism, I'm weighing whether contributing to signal cooperation is worth it, but calculating that being the lone contributor while others defect leaves me far worse off than defecting myself (-12 vs 2), so unilateral generosity is risky unless reciprocated.

Working through the marginal math confirms the derivative of my payoff with respect to keeping tokens is positive, meaning keeping is the individually dominant choice every round regardless of what others do, even though full group cooperation would yield more per person than full defection. Since there's no enforcement mechanism, I'm leaning toward defecting (keeping all tokens) as the rational play.
